articles.title: Previewing Every MLB Team's Biggest '26-27 Offseason Decision
articles.summary: It goes without saying that the biggest offseason decision that will affect all 30 teams will be the new collective bargaining agreement. Obviously, whether there's a salary cap and/or floor will go a long way in deciding how the offseason plays out.
articles.body:
It goes without saying that the biggest offseason decision that will affect all 30 teams will be the new collective bargaining agreement. Obviously, whether there's a salary cap and/or floor will go a long way in deciding how the offseason plays out.

What some people seem to be forgetting, though, is that the owners aren't able to lock the players out until after this current CBA expires on Dec. 1 at 11:59 p.m. ET. That means there will be close to a month of free agency before the lockout. With uncertainty about what the landscape will look like after the lockout, free agents might be more inclined to make quick decisions this offseason.

So with all that in mind, here's a preview of every MLB team's biggest 2026-2027 offseason decision.

Tampa Bay Rays: Will Nick Martinez return?

In his age-35 season, Nick Martinez was a first-time All-Star. He's 14-4 with a 2.92 ERA for a Rays team that's trending towards being the No. 1 seed in the AL playoffs.

His contract includes a mutual $20 million option for 2027. A general rule of thumb is that one side almost always declines a mutual option. Martinez may do that because he'll get paid a $4 million buyout if either side declines it. You also can never be sure how the Rays will choose to spend their limited budget. But dare we say, this could be a mutual option that both sides pick up.

New York Yankees: What does the future hold for Jazz Chisholm Jr.?

Jazz Chisholm Jr. started off his contract year by declaring he hoped to join Shohei Ohtani in the 50/50 home club. Well, it's mid September and Chisholm—currently on the injured list with a right thumb sprain—does have 40 stolen bases, but he's hit just 19 home runs.

Of course, no one—probably even including Chisholm himself—actually thought he would go 50/50. But a year ago, he homered 31 times and posted an .813 OPS. He's regressed almost 100 points this year, with a .715 OPS.

If the Yankees extend a qualifying offer to Chisholm—which was worth $21.05 million last offseason—the 28-year-old would probably be wise to take it and hope for a rebound season in 2027.

Boston Red Sox: Will Sonny Gray's option be exercised?

Remember what we said above about how rare it is that mutual options get picked up? Here's another situation where it could be in play, as Gray's deal includes a $30 million mutual option for 2027.

Gray has been tremendous after being acquired from the St. Louis Cardinals last offseason. He's 17-5 with a 2.76 ERA across 156.2 innings, which will likely earn him his third career top-five finish in AL Cy Young Award voting. Even with major money committed to Ranger Suárez and Garrett Crochet in the rotation already, chief baseball officer Craig Breslow will probably pick up the team's half of the option.

The question is whether Gray will. Considering he'll pitch next season at 37, he's probably not going to get more than $30 million for 2027 as a free agent. However, if he declines the option, the Red Sox will owe him a $10 million buyout . So he could collect that buyout, try to get at least $20 million for 2027 and perhaps pursue a multi-year commitment. He has plenty to consider.

Toronto Blue Jays: How do they retool after disappointing season?

Even if the Blue Jays manage to sneak into the postseason in a weak American League, it's been a very disappointing 2026 after they came so close to winning it all a year ago. There's still some very nice pieces here, but general manager Ross Atkins is going to have to consider how to retool this team to get them back in the World Series picture for 2027.

The good news for the Blue Jays is that George Springer ($24.16 million) and Shane Bieber ($16 million) will be coming off the books. They also moved off Kevin Gausman ($23 million), Jeff Hoffman ($11 million) and Daulton Varsho ($10.75 million) at the deadline. So there will be money to spend in the offseason.

With Vladimir Guerrero Jr., Dylan Cease, Trey Yesavage, Ernie Clement, José Soriano and Louis Varland, the Blue Jays still have a good base. They need to retool the rest of their roster in the offseason.

Baltimore Orioles: Are they going to bring back Trevor Rogers?

Really, we could got more broad here and just ask where the O's go after their second consecutive disappointing season. They tried spending money last offseason, and while Pete Alonso is having a tremendous season, the Orioles are in the cellar of the AL East.

On a micro level, they opted to hold onto Trevor Rogers before the trade deadline, despite him being in a contract year.

Trying to determine his value could be difficult, though. He finished runner-up for NL Rookie of the Year with the Miami Marlins in 2021, and posted a 1.81 ERA across 18 outings for Baltimore last season. In between those two campaigns, though, he posted a 5.09 ERA in just 52 outings. This season, he's logged a career-high 157.2 innings, but done so with a 4.22 ERA.

The easiest solution would be for the Orioles to extend Rogers, 28, a qualifying offer and have him accept it. If not, things could get more complicated.

Chicago White Sox: How do they build on improbable breakout?

Two years after losing a staggering 121 games, the White Sox are competing for the AL Central title, and seem to have an impressive young core with Miguel Vargas, Munetaka Murakami, Chase Meidroth, Tristan Peters, Sean Burke and Colson Montgomery.

The question will be, how, if at all, do the White Sox try to capitalize on being ahead of schedule? Adding a veteran starting pitcher would make sense, whether it would be Michael King or Clay Holmes in free agency, or Sandy Alcantara or Logan Gilbert via trade.

A couple things to consider here are that Justin Ishbia is still at least three years away from being able to purchase a controlling stake in the White Sox from Jerry Reinsdorf, and that the team is trying to get a new stadium. So it's unclear how all-in ownership will be on spending for the 2027 season, although the 2026 squad has been intriguing.

Cleveland Guardians: Will they trade Steven Kwan?

The reality with the way that ownership in Cleveland operates is that as star players get closer to free agency, the team often trades them. They've flirted with moving Steven Kwan before, and with the two-time All-Star set to become a free agent after the 2027 season, this might be the offseason to pull the trigger.

Kwan struggled at the plate for about a year, but has hit .356 with an .878 OPS since the All-Star Break. He's won four Gold Gloves in left field, and has graded out very well in center field this year, with five defensive runs saved and six outs above average.

The 29-year-old should be coveted by teams with needs in the outfield that are looking for a player with strong ball-to-bat skills.

Minnesota Twins: Will they continue to try to compete?

A year after a summer firesale, the Twins added before this year's trade deadline, acquiring the aforementioned Hoffman, A.J. Minter and Dean Kremer to bolster their pitching staff.

Unfortunately, even in a terrible AL, the Twins aren't going to be a playoff team. Another tremendous season was halted by injury for Byron Buxton, who is set to undergo surgery on his right hip . Buxton has made pretty clear that he doesn't have any desire to be traded, and his continued injuries would make it difficult to facilitate a trade. But two-time All-Star Joe Ryan can become a free agent after the 2027 season, and the Twins could probably fetch a very nice return for him in the winter.

It's admirable that Tom Pohlad is trying to change his family's reputation and get the franchise back on track. In this case, though, the best long-term move might be to take a step back in the winter, unless he plans to give Ryan a long-term contract.

Detroit Tigers: Could they actually make a push to bring back Tarik Skubal?

Tarik Skubal has expressed a willingness to consider the Tigers in free agency, even after they traded the two-time defending AL Cy Young Award winner to the Los Angeles Dodgers before the trade deadline.

The reality is that Skubal, a Scott Boras client, likely said that knowing that the Tigers won't make him a competitive offer in free agency, if they engage at all. If Mike Ilitch was still alive, they probably would. Chris Ilitch hasn't shown the same willingness to spend as his late father did.

Kansas City Royals: Are they really gonna hold onto Seth Lugo and Michael Wacha?

2026 is the second consecutive disappointing season for the Royals, but they resisted the temptation to trade either Seth Lugo or Michael Wacha before the trade deadline.

That suggests that general manager J.J. Picollo believes the Royals can compete in 2027. But there just hasn't been a ton of evidence since they were eliminated in the 2024 ALDS that this current group is capable of contending. And that makes it hard to justify carrying Lugo—who will turn 37 in November—and Michael Wacha, 35, into contract years.

Considering Lugo has a 5.76 ERA since the All-Star Break, it's probably going to be difficult to get anyone to take on his $21.5 million salary for 2027. Wacha will make $14 million in 2027, with a very affordable $14 million club option for 2028. There would definitely be teams interested in trading for him.

Houston Astros: Who will lead their front office?

The Astros parted ways with James Click after winning the 2022 World Series, so it's not particularly surprising they dismissed Dana Brown as general manager in August, even while they were in the midst of a race for the AL West title.

It's the worst-kept secret in the sport that Hall of Famer Jeff Bagwell has major influence in the organization, but he's done so without actually ever being the point person. Maybe it's time to just cut out the middleman and see if Bagwell could do the job himself.

Given the number of cooks in the kitchen and that winning a World Series wasn't enough for Click to keep his job, the Astros might have a difficult time getting the most attractive external candidates to be interested in this job.

Texas Rangers: Are they adding or subtracting?

The Rangers tried to deal Jacob deGrom before the trade deadline, only for the two-time NL Cy Young Award winner to block the deal . Would deGrom—owed $37 million in 2027, the final guaranteed season of a five-year deal—reconsider his stance in the offseason?

Even if deGrom doesn't intend to move, what will the winter look like for president of baseball operations Chris Young? Will the Rangers be aggressive in adding, or could they look to unload other stars? Corey Seager, Nathan Eovaldi, MacKenzie Gore, Josh Jung, Jake Burger and Jacob Latz are among the other pieces in Arlington that would be of interest to contending teams if available.

Seattle Mariners: Will they retain Randy Arozarena?

We mentioned the possibility of Gilbert being a trade candidate ahead of his contract year, but it's entirely possible the Mariners will choose to hold onto the All-Star righty and try to win with him, Bryan Woo, George Kirby and Emerson Hancock in the 2027 rotation.

President of baseball operations Jerry Dipoto will have to make a decision on Randy Arozarena. Giving him a qualifying offer is a no-brainer, but the former AL Rookie of the Year will surely decline it. The question then becomes do the Mariners offer Arozarena, 32 next season, four or five seasons, or do they let him walk in free agency?

For as disappointing as this year has been for the M's, Arozarena has been tremendous, as evidenced by his .849 OPS. However, he has a career .788 OPS, and there's risk in paying a guy after a career year.

Athletics: Who will lead their front office?

The Athletics probably never had enough pitching to compete in 2026. But if you knew entering the season that the AL West was going to be this weak, it wouldn't have been ridiculous to think the A's offense would keep them in the race.

That hasn't happened, and the Athletics ultimately fired general manager David Forst in August. That means they are looking for a new head of baseball ops, and frankly, it should be a pretty attractive position.

Between Nick Kurtz, Shea Langeliers, Tyler Soderstrom and Jacob Wilson, the A's aren't short on offensive talent. They're also expected to move to Las Vegas in 2028, and teams often spend big the offseason before going to a new stadium (and in this case, a new city).

Los Angeles Angels: Who will lead their front office?

If John Mozeliak wants to lead the Angels' front office on a permanent basis, the Halos would be wise to remove the interim tag and have the long-time St. Louis Cardinals' president of baseball operations steer the ship.

Make no mistake, though, this won't be an overnight fix. In the final days of the 2026 season, the Angels are trying to avoid losing 100 games. Even if they do that, they've clinched their 11th consecutive losing season. It will be the 12th year in a row that Mike Trout and company don't go to the postseason.

The good news is that Arte Moreno has agreed to sell the team to Stan Kroenke, who has had success as an owner in pretty much every sport. But it will take years for him to clean up the mess he's inheriting.

Atlanta Braves: Can they acquire a star pitcher?

MLB.com's Mark Feinsand reported that the Braves tried to trade Spencer Strider to the Rangers for deGrom prior to the trade deadline. That didn't ultimately come to fruition, but it might indicate that Alex Anthopoulos will be big-game hunting this winter.

Chris Sale is likely headed for another top-five finish in NL Cy Young Award voting, but he'll pitch next season at 38. The Braves have to plan for life after Sale, and even if they think he'll be really good for another year or two, they need another ace to pair with him.

Trading for Alcantara—more on him in a minute— or Gilbert would make sense. Freddy Peralta could also be someone that the Braves buy low on and rebuild after an ugly contract year split between the New York Mets and Rays.

Philadelphia Phillies: Who will be the manager?

While Don Mattingly has expressed a desire to return as the full-time manager for the Phillies in 2027, USA Today's Bob Nightengale reported in August that he'll need to guide the to at least a World Series appearance to be back.

When the Phillies fired Rob Thomson in April, president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski acknowledged the team tried to hire Alex Cora before ultimately naming Mattingly interim manager. Cora passed at the time, but it's pretty reasonable to assume Dombrowski is going to try to circle back this winter:

"I think Alex Cora is one of the finest managers in the game of baseball," Dombrowski said of Cora in April. "I've been fortunate enough to work with Hall of Fame managers like Tony La Russa and Jim Leyland. I've been very fortunate in my career. I think if Alex Cora decides to keep managing, he has a chance to be in that same category, that's how good he is."

Dombrowski and Cora were together in Boston when the Red Sox won the 2018 World Series, and it would seem to be a good bet the duo will be reunited in Philly next season.

Miami Marlins: Will they retain Sandy Alcantara?

The Marlins held onto Sandy Alcantara, arguably the greatest pitcher in franchise history, through the trade deadline. But it just feels like things are trending towards the former NL Cy Young Award winner getting dealt in the offseason.

First off, the Marlins will have to pick up his $21 million club option for 2027, which feels like a no-brainer. The two-time All-Star is once again back to being one of the game's elite workhorses, as he leads all pitchers with 205 innings pitched this season. He isn't necessarily as dominant as he was in 2022, but he has a 3.63 ERA since the All-Star Break, and his ability to log innings gives him a high floor.

Certainly, the Marlins could hold onto Alcantara and try to compete in 2027. Their history suggests that's unlikely though, because that would set up the possibility he walks in free agency after 2027 for nothing.

By all accounts, David Stearns will continue to be the president of baseball operations for the Mets, despite the fact that they're going to miss the playoffs with a top-five payroll for the second season in a row.

Stearns will have his work cut out trying to rebuild a roster he's at least partially responsible for tearing down. Before that happens, he'll also have to decide who will be the next manager. Interim manager Andy Green has a 35-34 record, but both he and Stearns have been pretty adamant that he'll be returning to the front office after the season concludes.

If it's not Green, Cora could also be a candidate, if he isn't hired by the Phillies. There's also going to be quite a bit of speculation about Hall of Famer Carlos Beltrán getting a crack at being skipper after being hired for that role and fired before ever managing a game in 2020 because of his involvement in the Astros' sign-stealing scandal. Beltrán is currently a special assistant to Stearns, as is J.D. Martinez, another intriguing name.

Washington Nationals: Will they consider offers for CJ Abrams and/or James Wood?

If the Nationals are planning to build around CJ Abrams and James Wood, they're getting to the point where owner Mark Lerner is going to have to authorize president of baseball operations to write some large checks. Since the late Ted Lerner passed away in 2023, the Nationals haven't been in the business of spending big money.

Until the Nationals sign both to long-term contracts, teams are going to call.

Abrams—whether you view him as a shortstop or second baseman—is one of the league's top infield bats. The 25-year-old two-time All-Star has two remaining arbitration years before he can become a free agent after the 2028 season. The Athletic's Spencer Nusbaum and Will Simmon linked the Yankees and Milwaukee Brewers to Abrams before the trade deadline, while Bob Nightengale of USA Today reported that the Red Sox were interested as well.

While the price to acquire Abrams would be steep, Wood would be even more expensive. He was an All-Star for the second year in a row, and currently leads the NL with a .395 on-base percentage. The 23-year-old can't become a free agent until after the 2030 campaign.

Milwaukee Brewers: Will they trade William Contreras?

Brewers fans don't want to think about it right now, but these could be the final weeks of William Contreras in their uniform. They'll surely pick up his $14.5 million club option for 2027, but they may look to trade him rather than carrying the three-time All-Star into his contract year.

If Contreras is indeed available, there will be widespread interest in him. The two-time Silver Slugger Award winner has an .805 OPS since the All-Star Break. Milwaukee president of baseball operations could move Contreras before his contract year, as he's done with Corbin Burnes and Peralta in recent offseasons.

The good news for the Brewers is that they've seen the likes of Burnes, Willy Adames, Devin Williams and Peralta depart in recent years, only for the train to keep on chugging. Even if Contreras isn't on the Brewers at this time next year, there's no reason to think manager Pat Murphy won't have Milwaukee in the playoff picture.

Chicago Cubs: Will they keep either of their top two outfield free agents?

Both Seiya Suzuki and Ian Happ will be free agents this offseason, and the Cubs may be hard-pressed to keep both.

Suzuki's fifth MLB season has probably been his best one, as he's homered 24 times and posted an .842 OPS. Perhaps most impressive is he's erased questions about his fielding with 14 defensive runs saved and four outs above average in right field this year. The Cubs will surely extend him a qualifying offer, but he'll just as surely decline it. The 32-year-old will then likely seek a deal of at least four years in free agency.

Happ, meanwhile, is the longest-tenured player on the team. The 32-year-old is in the final season of a three-year, $61 million contract. He's homered 23 times with a .740 OPS, while continuing to play strong defense in left field. He would probably accept a qualifying offer if saddled with one, so president of baseball operations Jed Hoyer might be unlikely to extend a QO. That likely means it will take another multi-year commitment to retain Happ.

Pittsburgh Pirates: Can they hold onto Brandon Lowe?

This year hasn't panned out how the Pirates hoped, but they can't blame Brandon Lowe for that. After being acquired from the Rays in an offseason trade, Lowe has homered 29 times and posted a 114 OPS+ (100 is league average).

Presumably, the Pirates will give Lowe a qualifying offer, and he'll likely turn it down. But being saddled with the QO and having an injury history may suppress Lowe's market. The 32-year-old would probably love to get a four-year deal, but two or three seasons seems more likely. Will Bob Nutting pony up to keep Lowe with the Buccos?

St. Louis Cardinals: Do they try to make a splash?

Entering the season, the rebuilding Cardinals seemed liked they could lose 90-plus games. They're still probably going to finish with a losing record, but Oli Marmol's squad has been much better than anticipated.

As it turned out, the Cardinals had better internal talent than we thought. Jordan Walker put everything together in 2026, while Alec Burleson and JJ Wetherholt look like long-term lineup cogs as well.

President of baseball operations Chaim Bloom has made his name off of player development, so he might not be inclined to swing a big trade this winter. But if he could land a pitcher with multiple years of control—Kirby and Cole Ragans are a couple names who come to mind—it might help the RedBirds return to contention in 2027.

Cincinnati Reds: Will they listen on Elly De La Cruz?

While it doesn't seem like there was ever traction, it is notable that Sean McAdam of MassLive reported that the Red Sox engaged the Reds about superstar Elly De La Cruz before the trade deadline.

You can bet that Boston and other teams will circle back this winter. And if there isn't a salary cap as part of the next CBA, the Reds may considering moving De La Cruz, who declined an extension offer bigger than Joey Votto's franchise record 10-year, $225 million deal before the 2025 season.

De La Cruz is still only 24, and the Reds have three arbitration years remaining with him before free agency. It's possible that even if this relationship ultimately ends with De La Cruz getting traded, it doesn't happen this offseason. But the possibility is certainly worth monitoring.

Los Angeles Dodgers: Do they re-sign Tarik Skubal?

There's only a handful of teams, if that many, who will be willing to spend the money it takes to sign Tarik Skubal in the offseason. The Dodgers will probably enter the offseason as the favorites to sign the two-time defending NL Cy Young Award winner.

With that said, the Dodgers haven't kept all their star players during the Andrew Friedman run, allowing Manny Machado, Seager, Max Scherzer and Trea Turner to leave in free agency for huge deals elsewhere. We don't know how they feel about Skubal.

Presumably, the Dodgers are very high on the lefty, who has a 2.52 ERA in eight starts in their uniform. However, he had NanoScope surgery on his elbow earlier this season, and is almost certainly going to want to top the $325 million that his current teammate Yoshinobu Yamamoto got in the largest guarantee ever for a pitcher. Maybe the Dodgers won't have the appetite to go that high for Skubal, who will turn 30 in November.

San Diego Padres: Is Michael King in their long-term plans?

It will be interesting to see whether new owners Kwanza Jones and José E. Feliciano authorize president of baseball operations A.J. Preller to be as aggressive as he's been under the Seidler Family. (Imagine if they tried to sign Skubal!)

One of the first interesting decisions the Padres will have is how to proceed with righty Michael King, who will probably opt out of the final two seasons of a three-year, $75 million contract. He'll be ineligible to receive the qualifying offer because he was saddled with it last offseason, so if he leaves in free agency, it will be for nothing.

King has eclipsed 30 starts for the second time in three seasons with the Padres, posting a 3.03 ERA. He's likely to garner at least four years as a free agent.

Arizona Diamondbacks: Is Ketel Marte still movable?

When Ketel Marte returned to the Diamondbacks in August after a restricted list stint turned into left knee inflammation, it felt like both sides had to just put on a good face for the rest of the season.

The problem is this isn't as simple as the Snakes deciding they are done with Marte in the offseason. By virtue of his 10-and-5 rights, Marte has a full no-trade clause. He can dig his heels in if he doesn't want to be traded.

Even if Marte is willing to move on, he's owed $82 million over the next four seasons, with a $13.5 million player option for 2031. That might have seemed team-friendly last offseason, but clubs who otherwise might have been interested likely will have some skepticism about Marte's character. It also doesn't help Marte's trade candidacy that he's posted a .758 OPS in 2026, a sharp decline from the .887 OPS he had from 2023 to 2025.

San Francisco Giants: What's Buster Posey's plan?

At 62-89, it's been a disastrous season for the Giants. President of baseball operations Buster Posey has already changed managers, so the heat is really on him heading into what could be a make-or-break offseason.

Rafael Devers had a rebound season, homering 37 times before a core muscle injury ended his season early. However, long-term deals given out to Matt Chapman and Adames already look like mistakes. Will ownership give him leeway to spend major money again this winter when his track record so far hasn't been great?

Alternatively, it would be interesting to see what the Giants could get for ace Logan Webb, who has two years left on his contract, if they shopped him. That's extremely unlikely to happen, however.

Colorado Rockies: Will new ownership flex muscle early?

Carrie Walton Penner and Greg Penner—already owners of the Denver Broncos—are slated to take over controlling interest of the Rockies from Dick Monfort after the resolution of the new MLB CBA. If you're a Rockies fans, it's hard not to feel ecstatic about that.

Denver isn't a major market, but the Penner's are among the richest people in the world given their ties to the Walmart. Not only do they have the ability to lose money on team payroll, but they can overhaul the organization and spend more on scouting, analytics, training, etc.

Perhaps the ownership change won't truly be felt until the 2027-28 offseason, but the Penner's taking control of the Rockies could be a game-changer.

articles.title: The New York Yankees Have a Clear Path to an Even Better 2027 Roster
articles.summary: With one of baseball's largest payrolls, a roster filled with high-priced stars and an unrivaled franchise reputation, the New York Yankees are in a perennial state of World Series-or-bust.
articles.body:
With one of baseball's largest payrolls, a roster filled with high-priced stars and an unrivaled franchise reputation, the New York Yankees are in a perennial state of World Series-or-bust.

Simply making the playoffs, or even reaching the Fall Classic, does not constitute a successful season for an organization that has been searching for title No. 28 since they last hoisted the trophy in 2009.

With an 87-63 record, they have already clinched a playoff spot, but they are 3.5 games back in the AL East and on a collision course with the Boston Red Sox in the AL Wild Card Series once again.

Absolutely, simply getting to October is half the battle; then it's just a matter of getting hot at the right time. This is not the best team in baseball. The odds will be stacked against them when the MLB postseason gets underway.

So what's next if they come up short again?

Trent Grisham ($22.025 million) and Jazz Chisholm ($10.2 million) coming off the books give the club some financial flexibility. There's a case to be made that they don't need to reinvest any of that money on the offensive side of things.

They made their splashy addition when they acquired Luis García Jr. and his additional year of club control at the trade deadline, which paves the way for their Opening Day lineup to potentially look something like this:

DH Ben Rice LF Cody Bellinger RF Aaron Judge 1B Luis García Jr. CF Spencer Jones 3B Ryan McMahon SS George Lombard Jr. 2B Anthony Volpe C Austin Wells

At this point, it's reasonable to treat anything you get from Giancarlo Stanton as a bonus, rather than relying on him to fill a spot. Versatile José Caballero returns in the super-utility role, while Heliot Ramos serves as the fourth outfielder and a platoon option against left-handed pitching.

They could explore an upgrade at catcher like Ryan Jeffers, or kick the tires on a reunion with Gleyber Torres or another second baseman on the market. With a full season of García and a healthy Aaron Judge, that group has the potential to be a top-tier offense, even with some holes at the bottom.

Then there's the starting rotation, which could be the best in baseball in 2027 if everyone is healthy.

RHP Cam Schlittler RHP Gerrit Cole LHP Max Fried LHP Carlos Rodón RHP Will Warren/LHP Ryan Weathers

That's without even mentioning a healthy Luis Gil or rising prospect Elmer Rodríguez, so there's no reason for the Yankees to be part of the Tarik Skubal sweepstakes or pursue any of the market's other top starting pitching options.

That leaves the bullpen, and outside of one breakout lefty, the Yankees will essentially be rebuilding from the ground up this winter. This is their chance to transform their roster into an October juggernaut.

Here's a look at every reliever who has made at least 30 appearances for the Yankees this season, along with their status for 2027:

RHP David Bednar — Free Agent RHP Jake Bird — Traded (WAS) RHP Paul Blackburn — Free Agent RHP Fernando Cruz — Injured, potential Tommy John RHP Camilo Doval — Traded (PIT) LHP Brent Headrick — Controllable through 2031 LHP Tim Hill — Free Agent LHP Ryan Yarborough — Free Agent

With a 1.94 ERA, 1.18 WHIP and 11.1 K/9 while logging 29 holds in 76 appearances, Brent Headrick has been one of the best relievers in baseball, but one standout setup reliever is not a bullpen. It's a good starting point, but this is a complete rebuild.

Already operating above the luxury tax threshold, the front office could simply tuck the savings from departing free agents into its pocket, lower its tax hit and cobble together a relief corps of low-cost veterans.

Or, they could build the best bullpen in baseball:

RHP Luis Gil RHP Carlos Lagrange (R) LHP Brock Burke (2 years, $10 million) RHP Jason Adam (1 year, $7 million) LHP Brent Headrick RHP Bryan Abreu (3 years, $30 million) LHP Adrián Morejón (4 years, $60 million) RHP David Bednar (3 years, $45 million)

With a 2.66 ERA, 10.1 K/9 and 34 saves in 37 chances, David Bednar has been one of the most reliable closers in baseball. Bringing him back should be a top priority. There are many talented bullpen arms on the market this winter, but few have his ninth-inning track record. The ones who do are on the other side of their prime, like Raisel Iglesias and Kenley Jansen.

Once the closer's role is solidified, Adrián Morejón and Bryan Abreu would provide a pair of high-octane setup arms with swing-and-miss stuff and multiple prime seasons left in the tank.

Morejón, 27, has a 2.87 ERA and 100 strikeouts in 81.2 innings this season, pitching off a fastball that averages 99.5 mph and a changeup that has generated a 54.1 percent whiff rate.

The Yankees actually made a push to acquire him at the deadline, with a package that reportedly included controllable starter Will Warren. He could come with a qualifying offer attached and a hefty AAV ask, but he's one of the best in the business.

Abreu, 29, is a bit more of a wild card, but one with massive upside.

After a terrific four-year stretch where he logged a 2.30 ERA and 12.7 K/9 across 275 appearances out of the Houston bullpen, he has pitched to a 3.86 ERA this season, partly due to a spike in his walk rate from 10.5 to 15.9 percent. However, his fastball-slider pairing remains elite. This down year might actually make signing both high-leverage relievers a more realistic goal.

Jason Adam (36 G, 2.51 ERA) and Brock Burke (73 G, 2.43 ERA) should come at a more reasonable cost. Adam because he missed time due to injury in 2026. Burke because he profiles more as a middle relief workhorse than a late-inning fireman on a contender. Both are quality additions that will be near the top of more than a few teams' shopping lists.

That leaves two open spots, one of which can be filled by Luis Gil, Ryan Weathers or whoever misses out on a rotation spot. The other spot gives hard-throwing top prospect Carlos Lagrange a clear path to make his case this spring.

Those projected contract figures add $52 million to the 2027 payroll. Not an insignificant number by any means, but it could be a small price to pay if it's what pushes this club over the top in October.

First things first, the Yankees have a 2026 playoff push to focus on. If they fall short of the ultimate goal once again, focusing their offseason efforts on building an untouchable relief corps could be the missing piece.

articles.title: Pete Alonso Given 300th MLB HR Ball By Mets Fans in Video After Trade for Signed Jerseys, More
articles.summary: Baltimore Orioles first baseman Pete Alonso exchanged some autographs for the 300th career home run ball he hit during Tuesday night's 7-5 road win over the New York Mets.
articles.body:
Baltimore Orioles first baseman Pete Alonso exchanged some autographs for the 300th career home run ball he hit during Tuesday night's 7-5 road win over the New York Mets.

SNY posted a video of Alonso meeting up with Mets fans Mike, Nick and Chris to make the trade. Alonso gave them autographed baseballs and bats, while also signing their jerseys. SNY noted that he brought them some beers and offered them tickets to O's games in Baltimore as well:

Alonso, 31, spent his first seven seasons with the Mets, hitting a team-record 264 career home runs.

The Orioles signed Alonso to a five-year, $155 million contract in free agency this past offseason, and he has continued to rake in Baltimore, slashing .267/.362/.499 with 36 homers and an American League-leading 101 RBI.

Given the success he enjoyed with the Mets, Alonso was cheered at Citi Field when he reached the 300-homer milestone on Tuesday.

In fact, Alonso even received a curtain call, which is something usually reserved for home-team players.

Alonso discussed how much the warm reception meant to him, telling reporters , "I appreciate all the support for all the years I've been here, all the life I've lived here. Obviously, they're recognizing that and they appreciate that. It's a two-way street. Really appreciate it."

Adding to the importance of Alonso's 300th career home run on Tuesday night was the fact that it tied the game at 3-3 in the ninth inning.

Baltimore went on to win the game in 11 innings, improving its record to 74-78, while the disappointing Mets fell to 69-82.

The Orioles still have an uphill climb, but Alonso kept them in the playoff mix Tuesday, as they trail the Cleveland Guardians by three games for the final wild-card spot in the AL.

articles.title: Mets' Sean Manaea, More React to Fans' Cheers for Pete Alonso in Return, 'Crazy to Me'
articles.summary: New York Mets players were not exactly thrilled to hear the Citi Field crowd go wild when Pete Alonso hit a ninth-inning homer off Kodai Senga to tie the score in a game the Baltimore Orioles went on to win 7-5 in 11 innings.
articles.body:
New York Mets players were not exactly thrilled to hear the Citi Field crowd go wild when Pete Alonso hit a ninth-inning homer off Kodai Senga to tie the score in a game the Baltimore Orioles went on to win 7-5 in 11 innings.

Mets starter Sean Manaea told reporters after the game he understands fans in Queens feel strongly about Alonso, but their reaction to an opposing player hitting a homer was "crazy to me."

Playing in his first series at Citi Field as a visiting player, Alonso hit his 300th career home run in the stadium where he hit 123 long balls while playing for the Mets from 2019 to '25.

Alonso's reaction seemed to indicate he enjoyed the moment.

Mets shortstop Francisco Lindor said after Monday's game he was disappointed fans didn't give more appreciation to Jonah Tong, specifically after the rookie pitcher was booed for walking Alonso in the third inning.

"I think next time, they've got to give the pitcher a little more love, too," Lindor said .

Interim manager Andy Green told reporters the Mets need to not let external factors out of their control impact their performance on the field.

"People are free to do whatever they want to do on the field," Green said. "Our job is to never let anything external impact the way we go about playing the game. I think that's tough in certain circumstances. I think guys may struggle with that at times."

It's not a surprise Mets fans have had as much enthusiasm about Alonso's return as anything this season. There hasn't been a lot to cheer for in Queens with the team closing in on a last-place finish in the NL East for the first time since 2003.

The combined attendance of 63,097 at Citi Field for the first two games against the Orioles is the most for any two-game home stretch for the Mets since Aug. 18-19 against the San Diego Padres.

articles.title: World Series MVP, 'Star Wars' actress share Hallmark-movie love story after over 20 years of marriage
articles.summary: "Star Wars" actreess Ashley Eckstein's golden birthday date with No. 22 sparked a real-life Hallmark movie romance with World Series MVP David Eckstein.
articles.body: Ashley Eckstein, who is known as Ahsoka Tano in "Star Wars" and Jan Brady in "The Brady Bunch in the White House," knows something about Hollywood. So, when she says the story of meeting her husband, World Series MVP David Eckstein, is something out of a Hallmark movie, she is absolutely correct. The star-studded couple is coming up on 21 years of marriage, but their relationship began with just a look. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE A golden birthday David Eckstein had been overlooked his entire baseball career, both literally and figuratively, as he stands at 5 feet, 6 inches. The two-time All-Star knew he wasn’t the five-star prospect who was going to blow people away with his impressive power or sizzling arm. So, Eckstein created his advantages through his unbelievable attention to detail, relentless work ethic and ability to win the mental game on the baseball field. So, when Eckstein, whose extremely regimented game-day routine begins the moment he wakes up, lost focus for five seconds because he locked eyes with a beautiful young woman in the stands while at the top step of the dugout celebrating a run, he was mad. "Get focused on the game, I barked at myself, disappointed that I would ever let something break my concentration," Eckstein wrote in his book "Just Enough." "I couldn’t believe I had let a fan break my routine." A few weeks later, Los Angeles Angels Vice President of Communications Tim Mead called Eckstein with a pitch. A publicist reached out to him wanting Eckstein to go a movie premiere with an actress. These types of pitches to Mead, or attempts to set Eckstein up on a date, weren’t uncommon. In fact, Mead normally deleted most. But not this one. Eckstein was apprehensive about the situation and looking for a way to get out of it, but Mead was firm. He had a feeling and urged Eckstein to call. After some research with his sister, Christine, Eckstein decided to pick up the phone and call. While the call went well, Eckstein told Ashley Drane he wouldn’t go to the premiere. Not until he met her in person beforehand. The Angels were out of the postseason hunt, but the season was still going on. Drane was filming an episode of "That '70s Show." While the timing wasn’t just ideal, it ended up being perfect. They settled on Monday, which was Drane’s 22nd birthday. And Drane’s 22nd birthday wasn’t just any birthday. It was her golden birthday. "In fourth grade, my fourth grade teacher told the whole class. He said, ‘Something special will happen on your golden birthday. Like when you turn 10 on the 10th. Well, my birthday is September 22nd and so ever since I was 10, I was waiting for my golden birthday when I would turn 22 on September 22nd," Ashley told OutKick in a recent interview. "And I believed him that something special would happen. Well, I didn't try for it. But because he didn't agree to go to the premiere and he said, ‘I have to meet you prior, the only day we both had free to meet was my golden birthday.’ So, I had a date with number 22 on my golden birthday, September 22nd when I turned 22." David, through his prudent research with Christine, discovered it was Ashley’s birthday and brought a gift. He was also wary of the Hollywood star potentially turning her nose up at his car. David was driving an "old clunker" with 150,000 miles on it, but that didn’t bother Ashley at all. In fact, it was Ashley’s car that told David all he needed to know. "It probably started when she pulled up in her old Toyota Corolla that had the missing door handle, the duct tape on it because then I was like, ‘OK, she's real. That's the type of girl that I could see myself with,’" David told OutKick. "Once I met her that night, we kind of knew." A couple of months after they started dating when Ashley told David a secret she had been keeping. She was the girl in the stands who broke David’s fierce concentration in the dugout. What David didn’t know? Ashley attended that game wearing her favorite number, Eckstein’s jersey number, No. 22. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Romance as a team Relationships and romance are hard in general, but especially so when both people in a relationship have incredibly demanding schedules. David, a professional baseball player, and Ashley, a Hollywood actress, had to work as a team to make it work. David, like the excellent leadoff hitter he was throughout his 10-year career, took the same approach to his relationship and set the tone early. "David from the very beginning, he said, ‘I'm going to let you know I don't play games. I like you and I'm going to be very upfront with you from the beginning,’ and he said if we're going to do this together I just want you to know we're a team and he said what I do is a reflection of you and what you do is a reflection of me so moving forward if we're in this we need to think of each other with every action and everything we do," Ashley said. "And I really appreciated that because it totally changed my mindset and we have — we've been a team ever since." David said that once you find your best friend, you can work through anything. For the two-time World Series champion, that meant Ashley had to sit through a baseball season with him. "The other thing I said early on, and this is why I did not put a ring on her finger earlier, was you need to sit through a baseball season with me because I'm a different person because once baseball season starts. I'm so locked in, but I need you to understand that that part of that time is very precious to me, but it doesn't mean I'm not thinking of you and don't care for you," David said. David’s rigid approach to baseball made him appreciate Ashley’s similar outlook toward acting. "I also understood her roles when she goes on set, because of my baseball career, I understand what she's doing. So, I thought it was actually a perfect mix for us to balance both worlds of her being the actress and me being a baseball player and but when we get to together, we really enjoy our time," David said. Ashley understands that romance is so much more than what is portrayed on TV and in movies. It’s about being there for the other person even when it doesn’t look pretty. "You put each other first and if you go into it with that mindset you're both going to be taken care of. I also joke with him sometimes romance just — it looks different. Sometimes romance is just him getting up to get me coffee when I have a busy day or doing the dishes. Yes, sometimes romance novels and romcoms, they give you a version of romance in your head and you think that that's what every day is like, yeah, but no, sometimes romance is just show — continuing to show up for someone, even when it just doesn't look pretty," Ashley said. "But when he was going through a rough time one season, I didn't know what to do for him. But I knew he liked fried chicken. And so, I found the perfect recipe. So, when he came home, even if it was a bad game, it was the perfect fried chicken. It’s just showing up for that person and putting each other first." Sacrificing for love While the beginning David and Ashley’s relationship was out of a fairytale, reality hit them hard. In 2008, David was with the Toronto Blue Jays and in the midst of a difficult season, and the two poured into each other and God. "I'll never forget there was one season. I mean, I'll say it. He wasn't happy. It was when he was with Toronto," Ashley said. "2008 was just a really hard, hard season. It was a hard season. And, um, nothing made sense. Absolutely nothing made sense. And what led up to that moment was horrible. I mean, some horrible things happened to him. And I just remember both of us, he didn't cry, but you could tell he was in despair. He was at at very low point. A very, very low point. And we both sat in church and he was silent and I just cried and and we had no other nothing else to do other than just say, 'Okay, it's all right. All right, God, it's in your hands.’" "‘Whatever, whatever you want, we will go wherever. We will do whatever. We're going to do it together. But we just sat there in desperation and said, ‘Okay, whatever is meant to be is meant to be.’ And then he got traded." Toronto wasn’t easy for Ashley either. If she wasn’t aware of just how ruthless Hollywood was, she found out when she moved north of the border to be with David. "I did end up walking away from my career, but he always came first, and he in turn, he's always put me first and it worked out, but it is hard. It's hard," Ashley said. "All of my agents and managers dropped me. I was a full-time working actress, live action, television, series regular. I mean, I had a lot and then just like that they were just like, ‘Oh, you can't be here. You can't audition. You're not flying in on every whim.’ Well, literally the exact quote was, ‘If you're not auditioning, you're not making money. And if you're not making money, you're no good to us.’ And then like that, I had nobody." David played two more seasons after he was traded from Toronto and retired. Not because no one wanted him, as he had more contract offers in free agency than he ever had before, but because it was his turn to support her. "I actually had more contract offers in 2011 than any other time I was in free agency but I had made the decision. Ashley had started her company ‘Her Universe’ and she basically she gave up her career as an actor. They all gave up on her when she made the move to Toronto to come be with me," David said. "I had made a decision that I was going to go be with her after the 10th year. And so, yeah, I walked away from all the contract offers even during the season and even after the 2011 season, I got called again to come back and play, but I already made the decision. Yeah. And we went out and created ‘Her Universe.’" For Ashley, it all ended up working out in the end, as "Star Wars" came along around that time, and she called what happened "the biggest blessing." ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW! Becoming authors In addition to being an actress and a former athlete, Ashley and David now have another title: authors. The couple wrote books and released their "his-and-hers" books on Sept. 8. David’s is a memoir called "Just Enough," while Ashley’s is called "Lucky 22." David always knew he wanted to write a book once he was done playing; it just took about 15 years after his playing days. Ashley’s inspiration for writing the book stemmed from a "crazy idea." "I just had a crazy idea. Once we started working with Blue Box Press and since they specialize in romance, how David and I met really is like a Hallmark movie. We didn't try for it that way. It just happened that way. And whenever we tell the story, everyone always says that's a Hallmark movie. That — that needs to be a Hallmark movie. And so it's only one chapter in David's book and it only deserves to be one chapter because he has a lot of story to tell. But I had a feeling that people are going to want to know more," Ashley said. "So I went to Liz and Jillian, the owners of Blue Box Press, and I said, ‘Okay, I have a crazy idea, but what if we do a his and hers version and what if we do a romance novel, Lucky 22, inspired by our true love story.’ So, mine is fiction, but it is very much inspired by our true story. And it's about 90% true." For David, reading Ashley’s book allowed him to see things from her perspective and reflect on who he was. "It was very interesting for me because she told it from her perspective like how it all came about of meeting me and I really realized how really regimented I was and how I was so focused on my career and my routine and stuff and then seeing it from her side of it, the opposite side. Kind of being all lonely going through this world where everyone thinks it's so glamorous and having to fight through it and stuff," David said. "It definitely brought some tears to my eyes. It definitely made me reflect on the person I was during that time period because in the sense of like I was so focused in on my career and being the best husband at that time in my mind thought I had needed to perform on the baseball field." On the flip side, Ashley called David’s story the "greatest underdog story" that had yet to be told. While the book runs through David’s World Series run with the St. Louis Cardinals in 2006, Ashley said it’s just as much about life than it is about baseball. "People think they know his story. They think, you know, they know him as the scrappy player that had heart and, you know, the little engine that could, you know, David versus Goliath. They think they know his story, but they truly don't know everything that he went through. And the beautiful part about his story is you don't need to know anything about baseball to be inspired by Just Enough. In fact, many people that have read it, our publishers, they know zero about baseball. And that — everyone like they call with tears in their eyes. Literally, our publisher is — who is a good friend of ours. She called and apologized. She goes, ‘I'm your friend.’ And I can't believe I didn't know everything you went through," Ashley said. This is a book about family, faith, also faith in yourself, and never giving up and perseverance and it can relate to everyone." The power couple also may have etched their names into the history books. "I don't think there's been another husband and wife that have dropped a book on the same day," Ashley said.

articles.title: MLB's most electric slugger just had one of the slowest, most disrespectful walk-off home runs of all time
articles.summary: Junior Caminero's 41st homer sealed a 2-1 Rays win over the A's, but his 40-plus-second home run trot stole the show and sparked AL MVP talk.
articles.body: Tampa Bay Rays phenom Junior Caminero is making a serious run at the AL MVP, but all fans saw Tuesday night was quite possibly the slowest walk of all time. Maybe this is what hitting a "walk-off" home run truly means? I don't know. If so, the 23-year-old nailed it. EX-MLB PITCHER GIVES HIS TAKE ON METS RELIEVER JEFRY YAN'S WILD STRIKEOUT SPLIT CELEBRATION Caminero hit his second walk-off in the span of five days Tuesday against the A's, wrapping his 41st home run of the year around the right field foul pole to win the game, 2-1. The superstar slugger is now hitting .279 this season to go along with the 41 dingers, along with 96 RBI and a nearly .900 OPS. For most of the season, the AL MVP has been Yordon Álvarez's to lose. And the Houston slugger hasn't lost it, by any means. But Caminero is on the verge of ripping it away — and his home run trot after Tuesday's walk-off may have sealed the deal. Take a look: Junior Caminero took forever to complete this trot Goodness gracious. I grew up watching David Ortiz absolutely milk home run trots, but I'm not sure I've ever seen one quite like that. Are you even allowed to touch the runner before he hits home? They're all just high-fiving him down the first base line. We grew up being SCOLDED if we dared touch a batter before he touched home. It was basically a sin. Apparently, that's just a myth — at least in the MLB rulebook. A deeeeeeeep dive actually revealed that there is no rule in MLB on this, but it's actually pretty strictly enforced down in the college ranks. ASTROS PLAYER BELTS HOME RUN, ROUNDS THE BASES AND THEN GETS DEVASTATING NEWS AFTER TOUCHING HOME Rule 5, Section 2 states: After a home run, no offensive team member, other than the base coaches, shall touch the batter-runner before home plate has been touched. No such rule exists in Major League Baseball. True story. The more you know! Anyway, Caminero's blast gave the Rays their 91st win of the year. Tampa has already clinched a playoff spot, and will likely wrap up the AL East here in a few days. As for the 40+ second trot, most on social media loved it. articles.title: Former MLB Draft Pick Cam Schiller Banned from Softball for 3 Years After Steroid Doping Violation
articles.summary: Former MLB draft pick Cam Schiller won't be able to play for USA Softball for three years due to a failed steroid test.
articles.body:
Former MLB draft pick Cam Schiller won't be able to play for USA Softball for three years due to a failed steroid test.

The International Testing Agency announced Wednesday that Schiller has accepted a three-year ban for violating the organization's anti-doping policy.

Per the ITA, Schiller tested positive for norandrosterone in a sample collected on July 13, 2025. He was provisionally suspended the following month and a B sample confirmed the presence of the same steroid.

Previewing Every MLB Team's Biggest Offseason Decision 🔮

By agreeing to accept the ban, Schiller's suspension was reduced by one year from four to three. He will be eligible to return on Aug. 7, 2028.

The ITA also announced Schiller's individual results from the 2025 WBSC Men's Softball World Cup, when his sample was originally collected, will be disqualified, including medals, points and prizes.

Schiller hit .450/.500/.700 in six games for Team USA during the 2025 WSBC Men's Softball World Cup. The United States defeated Japan 10-1 in the bronze-medal game.

An infielder who played college baseball at Oral Roberts, Schiller was a seventh-round draft pick by the Texas Rangers in 2012. He played two seasons in Low-A before shifting to softball.

Schiller has played for the U.S. in the WSBC Men's Softball World Cup three times since 2019. He won a bronze medal with the team in 2022.
